notes.text:
And set me down — So it seemed to me in the vision. Which is a lively representation of a threefold resurrection:

1. Of the resurrection of souls, from the death of sin, to the life of righteousness:

2. The resurrection of the church from an afflicted state, to liberty and peace:

3. The resurrection of the body at the great day, especially the bodies of believers to life eternal.
And he — The Lord.

Prophesied — Declared these promises. As I prophesied - While I was prophesying. A noise - A rattling of the bones in their motion. A shaking - A trembling or commotion among the bones, enough to manifest a divine presence, working among them. Came together - Glided nearer and nearer, 'till each bone met the bone to which it was to be joined. Of all the bones of all those numerous slain, not one was missing, not one missed its way, not one missed its place, but each knew and found its fellow. Thus in the resurrection of the dead, the scattered atoms shall be arranged in their proper place and order, and every bone come to his bone, by the same wisdom and power by which they were first formed in the womb of her that is with child.
Came up — Gradually spreading itself.
Prophesy — Declare what my will is. O breath - The soul, whose emblem here is wind; which, as it gently blew upon these lifeless creatures, each was inspired with its own soul or spirit.
And the breath — The spirit of life, or the soul, Gen. ii, 7.
The whole house — The emblem of the house of Israel. Are dried - Our state is as hopeless, as far from recovery, as dried bones are from life.
I will open — Though your captivity be as death, your persons close as the grave, yet I will open those graves.
Mark — Observe them accurately and punish them as they deserve. Stand - At thy tribunal.

Forgiveness — Thou art able and ready to forgive repenting sinners. Feared - Not with a slavish, but with a childlike fear. This mercy of thine is the foundation of all religion, without which men would desperately proceed in their impious courses.
I wait — That he would pardon my sins.
They — Whether soldiers that keep the night-watches in an army, or the priests or Levites who did so in the temple.

Israel — Every true Israelite. Plenteous - Abundantly sufficient for all persons who accept it upon God's terms. David testifies his humility, and exhorts Israel to trust in God, ver. 1-3. A song of degrees of David.

glossa.text:
*A canticle of degrees.* ((ID.)) The eleventh degree, etc., *as far as* a glad conclusion is set down with the certainty of pardon, there, *Let Israel hope in the Lord.*

*Out of the depths.* ((AUG.)) He who feels himself in the deep, etc., *as far as* as the Scripture says: *The sinner, when he shall have come into the depth of vices, contemneth.*

*Who shall abide it.* ((ID.)) Because well nigh all human life is barked at round about by sins, and every conscience is accused by its own thoughts. That heart is not chaste which presumes upon its own justice. Let it therefore presume upon the mercy of God, *For with him there is propitiation,* whence he subjoins:

*For with thee there is propitiation.* As it were: In what hope dost thou cry? Because there is mercy in thee, wherefore he speaks thus: Or join it thus.

((AUG.)) No man can abide it, etc., *as far as* one hope therefore there is: *For with thee there is propitiation,* etc., *For thy law's sake,* ((ID.)) I have waited for the *law* of mercy, etc., *as far as* and thou hast given this law in the very necessity.

*The morning.* ((ID.)) Let him hope in the morning watch who hopes for nothing else from God than immortality. *From the morning watch,* etc., *as far as* thence in the law the head and the tail of the victim were offered to the Lord. *Let Israel hope in the Lord.* ((CASS.)) The second part, where is the glad conclusion: Secure concerning himself, he preaches that they should hope always in the Lord. As it were, as his soul has hoped, so let Israel hope.
*And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities.* ((ID.)) Here he has now said what that one shall do, whom he called merciful and plentiful.

notes.text: For to be carnally minded — That is, to mind the things of the flesh. Is death - The sure mark of spiritual death, and the way to death everlasting. But to be spiritually minded - That is, to mind the things of the Spirit. Is life - A sure mark of spiritual life, and the way to life everlasting. And attended with peace - The peace of God, which is the foretaste of life everlasting; and peace with God, opposite to the enmity mentioned in the next verse.
Enmity against God — His existence, power, and providence.
They who are in the flesh — Under the government of it.

In the Spirit — Under his government. If any man have not the Spirit of Christ - Dwelling and governing in him. He is none of his - He is not a member of Christ; not a Christian; not in a state of salvation. A plain, express declaration, which admits of no exception. He that hath ears to hear, let him hear!

Now if Christ be in you — Where the Spirit of Christ is, there is Christ. The body indeed is dead - Devoted to death. Because of sin - Heretofore committed. But the Spirit is life - Already truly alive. Because of righteousness - Now attained. From ver. 13, St. Paul, having finished what he had begun, chap. vi, 1, describes purely the state of believers.

glossa.text: *For the prudence.* He who savours these things which are of the flesh is not just; for the prudence of the flesh is death. *Life and peace.* Life indeed referred to this, *the affection of the flesh is death;* but peace to that which follows: *the affection of the flesh is enmity toward God.*

*Because the wisdom of the flesh.* By enumerating these things he deters from obedience to the flesh.

*It is an enemy.* While it thinks God can do nothing beyond what is seen in the natures of things.

*If yet.* He speaks ambiguously, because they are not yet of perfect faith, but there is hope of their being perfected. *The Spirit of God.* The Spirit of Christ, because the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are the same.

*The body indeed.* By the name of the body he signifies the whole man, as Ezekiel conversely by the name of the soul, when he says: *The soul that hath sinned,* etc. And the sense is: If the spirit of Christ is in you, although the body be dead, that is, although the man be dead because of sins, that is, in sins, yet the spirit, that is, the soul which had been ungodly, lives: because it is joined to God, who is life, and this because of justification, that is, the remission of sins, which is from the Holy Spirit. *Dead,* he says, not mortal. For before sin the body was animal, that is, mortal, namely able to die. But which it was not necessary to die: now it is called dead because of sin, that is, because it is necessary to die. *Because of sin* to be shunned, this weakness is kept back, that thereby he may the more fear to sin.

*But if the Spirit. ((AUG.))* Mark that the Holy Spirit, etc., *as far as* even as who shall declare the generation of the Son?

*He shall quicken also your mortal. ((ID.))* Behold the fourth act. In the first action, etc., *as far as* because we had forsaken God who is above us.

*Mortal.* Not dead, because in the resurrection, when this mortal shall put on immortality, not only the necessity of dying, which it now has because of sin, but not even the mortality which the animal body had before sin, shall remain.

*Because of him that dwelleth.* It appears most evidently that man deserved, because of sin, the death not only of the spirit but also of the body, and that through the Holy Spirit both were delivered by Christ.

notes.text: One Lazarus — It is probable, Lazarus was younger than his sisters. Bethany is named, the town of Mary and Martha, and Lazarus is mentioned after them, ver. 5. Ecclesiastical history informs us, that Lazarus was now thirty years old, and that he lived thirty years after Christ's ascension.
It was that Mary who afterward anointed, &c. She was more known than her elder sister Martha, and as such is named before her.

This sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God — The event of this sickness will not be death, in the usual sense of the word, a final separation of his soul and body; but a manifestation of the glorious power of God.
Let us go into Judea — From the country east of Jordan, whither he had retired some time before, when the Jews sought to stone him, chap. x, 39, 40.

Are there not twelve hours in the day? — The Jews always divided the space from sunrise to sunset, were the days longer or shorter, into twelve parts: so that the hours of their day were all the year the same in number, though much shorter in winter than in summer. If any man walk in the day he stumbleth not - As if he had said, So there is such a space, a determined time, which God has allotted me. During that time I stumble not, amidst all the snares that are laid for me. Because he seeth the light of this world - And so I see the light of God surrounding me.
But if a man walk in the night — If he have not light from God; if his providence does no longer protect him.

Our friend Lazarus sleepeth — This he spoke, just when he died. Sleepeth - Such is the death of good men in the language of heaven. But the disciples did not yet understand this language. And the slowness of our understanding makes the Scripture often descend to our barbarous manner of speaking.
Thomas in Hebrew, as Didymus in Greek, signifies a twin. With him — With Jesus, whom he supposed the Jews would kill. It seems to be the language of despair.
Mary sat in the house — Probably not hearing what was said.
Whatsoever thou wilt ask, God will give it thee — So that she already believed he could raise him from the dead.
l am the resurrection — Of the dead. And the life - Of the living. He that believeth in me, though he die, yet shall he live - In life everlasting.
She fell at his feet — This Martha had not done. So she makes amends for her slowness in coming.

He groaned — So he restrained his tears. So he stopped them soon after, ver. 38. He troubled himself - An expression amazingly elegant, and full of the highest propriety. For the affections of Jesus were not properly passions, but voluntary emotions, which were wholly in his own power. And this tender trouble which he now voluntarily sustained, was full of the highest order and reason.
Jesus wept — Out of sympathy with those who were in tears all around him, as well as from a deep sense of the misery sin had brought upon human nature.
Could not this person have even caused, that this man should not have died? — Yet they never dreamed that he could raise him again! What a strange mixture of faith and unbelief.

It was a cave — So Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and their wives, except Rachel, were buried in the cave of Machpelah, Gen. xlix, 29-31. These caves were commonly in rocks, which abounded in that country, either hollowed by nature or hewn by art. And the entrance was shut up with a great stone, which sometimes had a monumental inscription.
Lord, by this time he stinketh — Thus did reason and faith struggle together.
Said I not — It appears by this, that Christ had said more to Martha than is before recorded.

Jesus lifted up his eyes — Not as if he applied to his Father for assistance. There is not the least show of this. He wrought the miracle with an air of absolute sovereignty, as the Lord of life and death. But it was as if he had said, I thank thee, that by the disposal of thy providence, thou hast granted my desire, in this remarkable opportunity of exerting my power, and showing forth thy praise.
He cried with a loud voice — That all who were present might hear. Lazarus, come forth - Jesus called him out of the tomb as easily as if he had been not only alive, but awake also.

And he came forth bound hand and foot with grave clothes — Which were wrapt round each hand and each foot, and his face was wrapt about with a napkin - If the Jews buried as the Egyptians did, the face was not covered with it, but it only went round the forehead, and under the chin; so that he might easily see his way.
Many believed on Him — And so the Son of God was glorified, according to what our Lord had said, ver. 4.

glossa.text: *Now there was.* While he tarries beyond the Jordan, Lazarus falls sick, and the sisters send to him there. These sisters of Lazarus are a figure of the Jews already received into eternal blessedness, who for the healing of their brother, that is, for the rest still wandering in the darkness of ignorance, beseech the Lord out of their most familiar manner of acting. *Lazarus was sick.* Lazarus is a figure of the Jews who were weak in the faith of Christ: Martha and Mary signify the teaching of the good Jews.

*Behold, he whom thou lovest,* etc. Lazarus, by whom the sinner is signified, who is loved by the Lord, because he came not to call the just but sinners. The sisters are the sinner's good thoughts, which pray for the loosing of his sins.
*For the glory of God,* etc. That is, that the Son of God may be glorified. Behold, he calls himself God, against those who say that the Son of God is not God.
*He loved.* The Saviour of the sick and the raiser of the dead loved Lazarus, because he was sick and dead.

*Two days.* That the four days might be fulfilled. For on the first day, on which it was announced to him, the sick man died beyond the Jordan; for two days he remained: behold, three; but on the fourth day he came.
*Let us go into Judea.* Mystically: it signifies that faith is to return to the Jews at the end through Elias and Enoch.

*The disciples say to him.* Terrified, wishing to give counsel to their master that he should not die, as elsewhere Peter also: *Far be it from thee, Lord,* this shall not be unto thee. But as Peter is praised for what is another's: *Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jona, because the Father hath revealed it to thee,* he is blamed for what is his own: *Go back behind me, Satan, because thou savourest not the things that are of God, but the things that are of man.* So too he rebuked these, saying that he is the day in which they ought to walk lest they stumble, and that walking without him they stumble, as now unwilling that he should die who came to die for men. But he says that they are the hours which follow the day, not days, but the day enlightens them. Twelve is a consecrated number which remains complete: for when Judas was cast down, who did not shine among the hours, another is substituted.
*Are there not twelve hours. ((HIER.))* Christ is the day, and in another manner the apostles are the day, as Christ is, etc., *as far as* they are understood to be the twelve apostles.
*That you may believe.* Not that they should only now begin to believe, but that they might believe more robustly. For their faith was always increased by miracles.
*And he found. ((AUG.))* Mystically: there are four days of death. A man is born, etc., *as far as* but mercy does not leave behind even such as these.

*But now also I know.* This I know, that thou canst raise him if thou wilt; which I leave to thy judgment. But I do not presume, nor do I ask that thou raise him, since I know not whether the resurrection be useful to be done.

*Yea, though he be dead.* Jesus raised three dead men: one in the house, that is, in the heart; a second at the gate, that is, in the mouth; a third in the tomb, that is, in the deed and the habit of sinning. *He shall live.* As Abraham, Isaac and Jacob live, whose God he is called as of the living. The believer, though dead, lives, as the unbeliever, though living, is dead.

*Secretly.* Because if the Jews had heard that she had been called by Jesus, she would not follow, and so they would not see the miracle. But because they thought that they were going to their brother's tomb, they followed. *And calleth thee.* By reason of brevity in Martha's words he shows what was not said before, that is, that the Lord had called Mary.
*They followed.* The evangelist took care to relate this, that we might see what occasion brought it about that the resurrection of the man four days dead should have more witnesses.

*He groaned in the spirit.* Note the power: he himself groaned and troubled himself, whom another could not trouble, as he took upon himself all things of this kind because he willed it. And it signifies how greatly a man ought to be troubled when pressed by so great a mass of sin. But when the sinner, reckoning what good things of God he has received and what evils he has rendered, groans in spirit and is troubled, Christ groans in him and is troubled, because faith concerning Christ is Christ in the heart. But faith groans in a man while he rebukes himself for his sins.

*Where have you laid him?* He who though absent knew that he was dead knows also where he is buried; but speaking thus, he signifies that he as it were does not know the lost man; whence it is said: *I know you not ((Matth. VII))*. And: *Where is Adam? ((Gen. III.))*

*Jesus therefore,* etc. He shows the difficulty of the quickening of such a sinner. *Now it was a cave.* Morally: every sinner pressed by the mass of his sins and weighed down by his own law, and now stinking by his own evil habit, openly corrupts others by his bad example: the sisters are certain thoughts, because sometimes, thinking that he has done ill, he grieves.
*Lord, by this time he stinketh.* She feared that, the stone being taken away, the stench would rather be stirred up than her brother raised.

*But for the people,* etc. By these words he shows that he seeks the glory of the Father, as in his other works. For because according to his manhood he was less than the Father, he asks of him the raising of Lazarus, and therefore says that he was heard, and this for the sake of the bystanders, that they might so believe him the Son of God.

*With a loud voice.* He groaned, he wept, he cried out, because he rises with difficulty whom the mass of an evil habit presses; but nevertheless after the great voice he rises, that is, by the great grace of God he is quickened while he repents.

*And forthwith he came forth.* While the sinner despises, he lies buried; when he repents, he rises; when he confesses, he comes forth, as though going out of hiding into the open. *Loose him.* Christ by himself quickens within; to his ministers he grants the power of loosing.

hymns.title: If death my friend and me divide
Gracious God, as your Son wept with Mary and Martha at the tomb of Lazarus
O God, just as we look into a mirror to see any soiled spots on our face
Out of the depths I cry to thee
Out of the depths, O God, we call to you

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn, and I have said to you, “Let my son go, that he may serve me”; and you have refused to let him go. Behold, I will kill your son, your firstborn.’”
echoes.note: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn' grounds the sonship/adoption language of vv.14-17; the Spirit constitutes believers as 'children of God,' transferring Israel's sonship status to those led by the Spirit.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The Spirit enabling 'the ordinance of the law' to be 'fulfilled in us' (v.4) draws on the new-covenant promise to write the Torah on the heart, internalizing the law by divine agency rather than external command.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes' undergirds vv.4-9: the indwelling Spirit (vv.9,11) produces obedience and 'walking according to the Spirit'; the verbal cluster Spirit-indwelling-walking-statutes is distinctive to Ezekiel.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit in you and you shall live' (the dry-bones vision) lies behind v.11, where the Spirit who raised Jesus 'will also give life to your mortal bodies'; Spirit-giving-life-to-dead-bodies is the precise Ezekielian figure.

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]
echoes.note: 'The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace' and 'if you live after the flesh you must die... by the Spirit... you will live' (vv.6,13) reframe the covenantal life-and-death choice of Moses' exhortation set before Israel.

echoes.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'When Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son' supplies the adopted-son-led-by-God motif (vv.14-15); the tender father-son relation undergirds the cry 'Abba! Father!'

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: 'In the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, it shall be said, You are children of the living God' anticipates 'these are children of God' / 'we are children of God' (vv.14,16); Paul cites this very text in Romans 9:26.

echoes.text: if the anointed priest sins so as to bring guilt on the people, then let him offer for his sin, which he has sinned, a young bull without defect to Yahweh for a sin offering.
echoes.note: 'for sin' (peri hamartias) in v.3 reproduces the Septuagint's standing phrase for the sin offering; God's sending his Son 'for sin' figurally casts Christ in the role of the Levitical purification sacrifice that 'condemns sin in the flesh.'

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.”
echoes.note: The flesh/Spirit antithesis (vv.5-9), where 'flesh' marks mortal humanity opposed to God's enduring Spirit, faintly recalls 'My Spirit will not abide in man forever, for he is flesh.'

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: 'The spirit is alive' / God giving 'life to your mortal bodies' (vv.10-11) faintly evokes the breath of life animating dust-formed Adam, now reapplied as resurrection-life by the Spirit.

echoes.text: For you are our Father, though Abraham doesn’t know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us: you, Yahweh, are our Father; our Redeemer from everlasting is your name.
echoes.note: 'You, O LORD, are our Father' — Israel's corporate address of God as Father — stands behind the Spirit-prompted filial cry 'Abba! Father!' (v.15).

echoes.text: “But I said, ‘How I would put you among the children, and give you a pleasant land, a goodly heritage of the armies of the nations!’ and I said, ‘You shall call me “My Father”, and shall not turn away from following me.’
echoes.note: 'I thought you would call me My Father and would not turn from following me' — God's hope that adopted Israel address him as Father — resonates with the adoptive cry of v.15.

echoes.text: I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.
echoes.note: The covenant formula 'I will... be your God, and you shall be my people,' realized through the indwelling Spirit (vv.9-16), faintly underlies the divine-belonging and sonship affirmed by the Spirit's testimony.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Jesus' euphemism that Lazarus 'has fallen asleep' and will be awakened maps onto Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake,' the classic OT idiom for resurrection as awakening from sleep. Volume is moderate (shared sleep/awaken vocabulary) and coheres with the chapter's resurrection program. Availability secure as the seminal resurrection text.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: The 'sickness not unto death but for the glory of God' frames Lazarus' death as a stage on which divine life-giving will be displayed, echoing the Creator who breathes life into dust. Faint, but coheres with John's creation theology (1:1-4) and the breath-of-life motif that undergirds resurrection texts. Contested.

echoes.text: so man lies down and doesn’t rise. Until the heavens are no more, they shall not awake, nor be roused out of their sleep.
echoes.note: Job's 'man lies down and rises not till the heavens are no more; they will not awake nor be roused from their sleep' supplies the sleep-of-death idiom that Jesus inverts by awakening Lazarus. Coherence is good but volume is faint and the idiom is widely diffused. Contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: Behold, and answer me, Yahweh, my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death;
echoes.note: 'Lighten my eyes lest I sleep the sleep of death' associates sleep with death and divine light, resonating with both the 'fallen asleep' euphemism and Jesus' day/night light saying (vv.9-10). Faint and idiomatic; offered honestly as low-confidence.

echoes.text: Give glory to Yahweh your God, before he causes darkness, and before your feet stumble on the dark mountains, and, while you look for light, he turns it into the shadow of death, and makes it gross darkness.
echoes.note: Jesus' walking-in-the-day-versus-stumbling-in-the-dark saying echoes the prophetic 'give glory to the LORD before he brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the twilight mountains.' Shared stumble/light/darkness imagery; coherence with Johannine light theme but low volume. Contested.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Martha's confession 'I know he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day' is precisely the Danielic doctrine of bodily resurrection at the end, the only OT text giving it explicit shape. High volume and recurrence; Jesus then collapses 'the last day' into his own person ('I am the resurrection'). Availability and coherence are strong.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: The whole Lazarus episode enacts Ezekiel's vision: God opens graves, raises the dead, and gives life by his Spirit/word so that 'you shall know that I am the LORD.' 'I am the resurrection and the life' figurally fulfills Yahweh's promise to raise the dead from their tombs. High volume of shared grave/raising imagery and strong coherence with the sign's purpose (that they may believe / know).

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust!' is the Isaianic resurrection promise underlying both Martha's last-day hope and the literal raising of Lazarus. Strong volume (dead-shall-live, awake-from-dust) and coherence with Daniel 12:2 cluster.

echoes.text: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? “Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.
echoes.note: 'Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol? Shall I redeem them from Death?' grounds the hope that death is not final, the hope Martha voices. Jesus as 'the resurrection and the life' answers Hosea's rhetorical challenge to Death. Moderate volume; coheres with the chapter's victory-over-death theme.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'I kill and I make alive' is the foundational divine self-claim that only God gives and takes life; Jesus' 'I am the resurrection and the life' assumes this prerogative in the first person. The 'I am' form coheres with the Johannine egō eimi sayings rooted in Deuteronomy/Isaiah self-declarations. Moderate volume.

echoes.text: “Yahweh kills, and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.
echoes.note: Hannah's 'The LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up' parallels Deuteronomy 32:39 as the OT confession of God's resurrection power that Jesus now wields. Coheres with the life-giving claim; moderate volume via the kill/make-alive pairing.

echoes.text: I will not die, but live, and declare Yah’s works.
echoes.note: 'I shall not die, but live, and recount the deeds of the LORD' resonates with Jesus' promise that the believer 'shall never die.' Faint verbal contact; offered as low-confidence given the Psalm's broader Passion-week use. Contested.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: Jesus 'troubled in spirit' and weeping, 'a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief,' figures the Servant who bears human sorrow. Coheres with the chapter's later substitution theme (Caiaphas, vv.50-52) and John's Servant Christology. Moderate volume via the grief/sorrow correspondence.

echoes.text: You number my wanderings. You put my tears into your bottle. Aren’t they in your book?
echoes.note: 'You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle' frames divine attentiveness to human weeping, resonating with Jesus weeping and being deeply moved at the tomb. Faint and thematic rather than verbal; coherence with the compassion motif but low volume. Contested.

echoes.text: Joseph fell on his father’s face, wept on him, and kissed him.
echoes.note: Joseph weeping over and mourning his dead father supplies a patriarchal precedent for righteous weeping over the dead, ambient behind 'Jesus wept.' Very faint, generic mourning topos; honestly low-confidence. Contested.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: The bystanders' 'this man who opened the eyes of the blind' recalls Isaiah's eschatological sign that 'the eyes of the blind shall be opened,' which John applies to Jesus' ch.9 sign. The cross-reference here invokes that Isaianic frame as proof of life-giving power. Low volume in this pericope; contested as a direct echo.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: The command 'Lazarus, come out!' and the dead man emerging from the cave-tomb enact Ezekiel's 'I will open your graves and raise you from your graves' brought to life by the word. The grave-clothes/loosing imagery and the loud summoning voice are strongly coherent with the dry-bones vivification by God's word. Highest-volume figural anchor of the chapter.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Elijah raising the widow of Zarephath's son is the foundational prophet-raises-the-dead type that Jesus surpasses; cf. the 'four days' to magnify the miracle. Strong recurrence (paired with Elisha) and coherence: a prophet's word/prayer restores a dead son to life. Availability secure.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha raising the Shunammite's son completes the prophetic resurrection pattern behind the Lazarus sign; the restored child and Jesus' restored friend share the dead-son-revived type. High recurrence with 1 Kings 17; coherence with John's portrayal of Jesus as the prophet greater than Elijah/Elisha.

echoes.text: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
echoes.note: Jesus' creative summons by 'a loud voice' that calls the dead into life echoes the divine word that calls being out of nothing ('Let there be light'), consistent with John's prologue identifying Jesus as the creative Word. Moderate volume; strong coherence with Johannine creation/word theology.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The bodily emergence of one who slept in the dust anticipates Daniel's awakening of those who sleep in the dust; Lazarus is a proleptic enactment of the last-day resurrection Martha named (v.24). Moderate volume here, reinforcing the chapter-wide Danielic frame.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; your dead shall live' is enacted as Lazarus is summoned from the dust of the tomb. The literal raising performs Isaiah's promise; moderate volume reinforcing the resurrection-promise cluster of the chapter.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t […]
echoes.note: Caiaphas' 'it is better that one man die for the people' unwittingly states the Servant's vicarious substitution: 'he was cut off from the land of the living for the transgression of my people.' John flags it as prophecy, making the one-dies-for-the-many a deliberate Isaianic atonement type. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, by the watercourses, and in all the inhabited places of the […]
echoes.note: 'Gather together into one the children of God who are scattered' enacts the shepherd-God's promise to 'seek out my scattered sheep and gather them from where they were scattered.' Strong volume on the gather/scatter vocabulary and coherence with John 10's shepherd theme. Availability secure.

echoes.text: Say to them, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I will take the children of Israel from among the nations, where they are gone, and will gather them on every side, and bring them into their own land: and I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all; and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all;
echoes.note: Following the dry-bones grave-opening, Ezekiel 37 promises to 'gather' the scattered Israelites 'and make them one nation' — precisely the gathering-into-one of v.52. The same chapter that grounds the resurrection sign grounds the ingathering, a tight intra-Ezekielian coherence. High volume.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: That Jesus would die 'not for the nation only but to gather the scattered children of God into one' echoes the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations' and to restore the dispersed of Israel, widening salvation beyond the nation. Moderate volume; coheres with John's universalizing of the death's scope.

echoes.text: that then Yahweh your God will release you from captivity, have compassion on you, and will return and gather you from all the peoples where Yahweh your God has scattered you. If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of the heavens, from there Yahweh your God will gather you, and from there he will bring you back.
echoes.note: 'He will gather you again from all the peoples where the LORD scattered you... from there he will gather you' is the covenantal ingathering-of-the-dispersed promise behind 'gather into one the scattered children of God.' Moderate-to-high volume on the scatter/gather diaspora language; coherence with the universal scope.

echoes.text: He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
echoes.note: 'He will assemble the banished of Israel and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth' supplies the eschatological-ingathering idiom for gathering the scattered children of God. Moderate volume; recurs with Deuteronomy 30 and Ezekiel 34/37 in the dispersion-gathering cluster.

echoes.text: I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they shall be fruitful and multiply.
echoes.note: 'I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them' parallels Ezekiel 34 in the shepherd-gathers-the-scattered motif behind v.52. Moderate volume, reinforcing the gathering theme; coheres with John's flock/shepherd imagery.

echoes.text: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive.
echoes.note: Caiaphas' malicious counsel that providentially saves many enacts Joseph's 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to keep many people alive.' The dramatic irony of unwitting prophecy producing salvation is strongly coherent; moderate volume via the evil-counsel-turned-deliverance pattern.

echoes.text: I will signal for them, and gather them; for I have redeemed them; and they will increase as they have increased. I will sow them among the peoples; and they will remember me in far countries; and they will live with their children, and will return.
echoes.note: 'I will gather them in... though I scattered them among the nations, yet in far countries they shall remember me' echoes the scatter/gather pattern of v.52. Faint relative to the stronger Ezekiel/Deuteronomy parallels; offered as low-confidence. Contested.

echoes.text: “‘So you shall not pollute the land in which you are; for blood pollutes the land. No atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, but by the blood of him who shed it.
echoes.note: The notion that the land/nation is preserved by a death ('no expiation for the land for blood except by the blood of him who shed it') faintly underlies Caiaphas' calculus that one death spares the nation. Low volume and contested as a deliberate echo.

harmony.title: The raising of Lazarus
harmony.note: John's climactic sign — "I am the resurrection and the life" — and in John the act that seals the plot to kill him.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Out of the depths we cry to you, O Lord.
With you there is forgiveness; our souls wait for you.
Can these bones live? Only you know, O God.
Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe.
Lazarus, come out; unbind him, and let him go.
You are the resurrection and the life.
Roll back the stone; come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: A valley floor white with bones, dry as chalk, picked clean by years; and a voice asking, mortal, can these live?
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Then a rattling, bone to its bone, sinew and skin, and the wind comes from the four corners and they stand and breathe.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Out of our own depths we wait for you more than the watchman waits for the morning; with you there is forgiveness.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
At a sealed grave you wept, and then you called a dead man by name, and he came out still wrapped in the cloths.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You are the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in you will live. Come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Breathe on us. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Out of the depths we wait for you, O Lord.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Come from the four winds, O breath, and let these bones live.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You call us by name from the grave: come out.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You are resurrection and life. Come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.
